tool_input.content:
Beadle: what it can do, and why you can trust it

A plain-language guide for the person who owns the mailbox — not the code.

Beadle runs in two very different modes

Everything about "can I trust this" comes down to one question: is a human watching when the action happens?

💬

You ask, Beadle does

Through Claude Code, right now, with you there.

You say "check my inbox" or "reply to Jim." Beadle looks at your mail, tells an AI assistant what it sees, and the assistant acts — but only because you just asked it to, this instant.

a human is watching
🤖

Beadle watches by itself

A background process, on a timer, with nobody at the keyboard.

Beadle checks the mailbox every few minutes on its own. It can quietly tell you something arrived, or — if you've set it up to — read, reply, archive, or even run a pre-approved task, without you doing anything.

nobody is watching
The rule of thumb: the less a human is watching, the more locks Beadle needs before it will act. Everything below is really just that one idea, applied four different ways.

How much should you trust an email?

Every message Beadle sees gets sorted onto one of four rungs, based on how hard it would be for someone to fake. This is completely separate from who the person claims to be — it's about whether that claim can be checked.

🔒
Sealed
Sent Proton-to-Proton, end-to-end encrypted. The strongest signal — this could not have been forged in transit.
✍️
Signed & checked
From outside Proton, but digitally signed, and the signature actually checked out against a known key.
⚠️
Signed, but broken
Claims to be signed, but the signature is invalid. Treat this as a red flag — someone may be trying to impersonate a known sender.
📨
Plain mail
No signature at all. Anyone can put anything in a "From:" line — this is exactly as trustworthy as an unsigned letter.

On top of that ladder, you control a second, separate switch per contact: can this person's mail be read, can Beadle reply to them, and can their mail trigger an automated task? A well-signed, sealed email from a stranger still can't do anything you haven't explicitly allowed.

What actually happens, scenario by scenario

You're watching

You ask Beadle to check your inbox

Beadle lists every message and labels each one with its trust rung. Nothing is acted on automatically — you read the list and decide what matters. This is the safest possible mode: you are the final check, every single time.

You're watching

You ask Beadle to reply to someone

Before treating the email's request as something worth acting on, two things have to be true: the message has to sit on the Sealed or Signed & checked rung, and that contact has to be someone you've allowed to reply to. A "Plain mail" or "Signed, but broken" message is shown to you as-is — described, never obeyed — even from someone you know.

Nobody's watching

Beadle notices new mail in the background

Running quietly, Beadle can simply tap you on the shoulder — "3 new messages" — and wait for you to look. No content is read out loud, nothing is decided; it just wakes up whatever is watching.

Nobody's watching

Beadle processes your inbox on a schedule

If you've turned this on, Beadle checks mail every few minutes and acts using the exact same two rules as above — trust rung, then contact permission — just without you present for each individual message. A stranger's unsigned mail still gets ignored the same way it would if you were watching.

  • Message must be Sealed or Signed & checked
  • Sender must be a contact you've granted reply/read access to
Nobody's watching · highest stakes

The background daemon runs a task triggered by email

This is the one case where mail can make Beadle execute something with zero human involvement, so it gets the most locks — three, not two:

  • Message must be Sealed or Signed & checked (same as above)
  • Sender must have "trigger tasks" permission, not just read/reply
  • The task itself must be a recipe you personally pre-approved and digitally signed — the email can only pick which approved recipe runs, it can never invent a new one or run an arbitrary command
That third lock exists because this is the only place a piece of paper on disk — a recipe file — turns directly into an action with no one double-checking it. If you never sign any recipes, this whole path is inert: it disables itself rather than guessing at what's safe. A recipe that's supposed to be locked but isn't quite configured right is treated as no recipes at all, never as "trust it anyway."

Quick reference

SituationCan it act without you?What stops abuse
You ask, liveNo — you see everything firstYou
Background notify onlyNo — just a nudgeNothing acts, so nothing to abuse
Scheduled inbox processingYesTrust rung + contact permission
Background daemon, email-triggered taskYesTrust rung + contact permission + your pre-signed recipe
For the technically curious

Trust rung = the four-level classifier (trusted/verified/untrusted/unverified) backed by PGP signature verification and Proton's end-to-end headers. Contact permission = the per-contact rwx bits you set in your address book. The pre-signed recipe lock is VerifySignature gating beadle-daemon's command loader (DES-034/035) — it only exists in the standalone background daemon, not in the interactive Claude Code tools, because that's the only place an on-disk file can turn into an executed action with nobody reviewing it first.

Beadle — GPG-signed instructions, owner-controlled, zero agent authority by default.

tool_input.content:
Beadle: what it can do, and why you can trust it

A plain-language guide for the person who owns the mailbox — not the code.

Two checks. Always. No exceptions.

Whether you're at the keyboard asking Beadle to check your inbox, or a background process is running unattended, the exact same two checks apply, every time, to every message. Nothing about being watched or unwatched changes this.

1

How well-verified is this message?

Can the claimed sender actually be proven — or could anyone have written that "From:" line?

2

What has the owner allowed this sender to do?

Even a fully verified sender can only do what you've explicitly permitted them to.

Check 1 — how well-verified is this message?

Every message lands on one of four rungs, based on how hard it would be to fake:

🔒
Sealed
Sent Proton-to-Proton, end-to-end encrypted. Could not have been forged in transit.
✍️
Signed & checked
Digitally signed, and the signature actually checked out against a known key.
⚠️
Signed, but broken
Claims to be signed, but the signature is invalid — a red flag, possible impersonation.
📨
Plain mail
No signature at all. As trustworthy as an unsigned letter — which is to say, not very.

Check 2 — what has this sender been allowed to do?

You set this per contact, independent of the ladder above. It's the same idea as file permissions:

r
Read — Beadle may look at their mail and surface it to you.
w
Write — Beadle may reply to them on your behalf.
x
Execute — their mail may trigger an automated task, not just a reply.

A sealed, perfectly-verified email from a total stranger still can't do anything — they have --- by default. Verification and permission are two separate locks, and both have to open.

Passing both checks: two very different things can happen next

This is the part that actually differs — not "is someone watching," but what kind of action a permission unlocks:

r / w — judgment

An LLM reads it and decides

Once a message clears both checks, its content becomes a prompt: an assistant reads what it actually says and decides how to respond, the same way it would if you'd typed the request yourself. This happens whether you triggered the check personally or a background poller did — the check doesn't care who woke it up.

x — fixed recipe

A pre-approved recipe runs

The background daemon works differently: a verified, permitted email doesn't get to freely instruct anything. It can only pick which of a small set of recipes runs — recipes you wrote and digitally signed ahead of time. The email supplies no new instructions, only a selection.

Why the recipe needs one more lock. Reading a message and using judgment has a safety net built in — an LLM can notice something's off. Running a fixed recipe has no such net: it just executes, exactly as written. So a recipe file gets a signature check of its own, once, when it's written — proving you authored it — completely separate from whether any individual email is trustworthy. Skip that setup entirely and this path does nothing at all, rather than guessing at what's safe. A recipe that's supposed to be locked but is misconfigured is treated as no recipes exist, never as "run it anyway."

Quick reference

What you're doingCheck 1 — verified?Check 2 — permitted?What happens
Reading your inboxShown, not required—You see everything, labeled; you decide
Getting a reply sentSealed or Signed & checkedwAn LLM reads the message and replies using judgment
Background inbox processingSealed or Signed & checkedr/wSame as above, just running on a timer instead of on request
Email triggers a background taskSealed or Signed & checkedxOne of your pre-signed recipes runs — nothing else can
For the technically curious

Check 1 = the four-level classifier (trusted/verified/untrusted/unverified), backed by PGP signature verification and Proton's end-to-end headers — identical code path in both binaries. Check 2 = the per-contact rwx bits in your address book (contacts.CheckPermission) — also shared. The recipe-signature lock is VerifySignature gating beadle-daemon's command loader (DES-034/035): it exists only where a fixed, on-disk artifact can be selected and run with no interpretive step in between, which today is only the standalone background daemon's recipe execution — not the interactive or scheduled read/reply paths, which always route through an LLM's judgment instead of running anything directly.

Beadle — GPG-signed instructions, owner-controlled, zero agent authority by default.

'Owner' is used throughout code and docs to name the single GPG fingerprint (daemon.json's owner_handle/owner_gpg_key_id) that internal/daemon.VerifySignature requires a command/recipe YAML file to be signed by. This term is misleading: it implies a privileged role governing the agent generally, when beadle has no such role -- power to direct the agent comes entirely from per-contact rwx permission grants (internal/contacts.CheckPermission), which have zero special-casing for any single party. The correct, precise concept is narrower: this key names the *authorizer* of a recipe -- whoever's signature makes a recipe file eligible to load and run at all. tool_input.content:
Beadle: what it can do, and why you can trust it

Beadle gives an AI agent its own email address. This is about that mailbox — not yours.

Whose mailbox is this?

Beadle isn't a tool that reads a person's personal inbox. It gives an autonomous agent (say, [redacted-email]) a mailbox of its own. Email becomes a channel people can use to send that agent instructions — from anywhere, without a live session. That's powerful, and it's exactly why it needs a real trust model: anyone who can get a message into that mailbox is, in some sense, talking directly to the agent.

Two checks. Always. No exceptions.

Every message that arrives in the agent's mailbox goes through the same two checks, whether a human is driving right now or a background process is running unattended:

1

How well-verified is this message?

Can the claimed sender actually be proven — or could anyone have written that "From:" line?

2

What has this specific sender been granted?

Being verified isn't enough on its own — the sender also needs an explicit grant for whatever they're asking the agent to do.

Check 1 — how well-verified is this message?

Every message lands on one of four rungs, based on how hard it would be to fake:

🔒
Sealed
Sent Proton-to-Proton, end-to-end encrypted. Could not have been forged in transit.
✍️
Signed & checked
Digitally signed, and the signature actually checked out against a known key.
⚠️
Signed, but broken
Claims to be signed, but the signature is invalid — a red flag, possible impersonation.
📨
Plain mail
No signature at all. As trustworthy as an unsigned letter — which is to say, not very.

Check 2 — what has this sender been granted?

There is no privileged "owner" role that sits above everyone else. Power to direct the agent comes entirely from grants set per sender, on a per-mailbox basis:

r
Read — the agent may look at this sender's mail and pay attention to it.
w
Write — the agent may reply to this sender.
x
Execute — this sender's mail may trigger an automated task, not just a reply.

Any number of different people or systems can each hold their own combination of these, completely independently — a teammate might have rw, a monitoring bot might have only r, a CI system might have x. Nobody is special by default; a sealed, perfectly-verified message from someone with no grant at all still unlocks nothing.

Passing both checks: two very different things can happen next

What actually varies isn't who's watching — it's what kind of action a grant unlocks:

r / w — judgment

The agent reads it and decides

Once a message clears both checks, its content becomes something the agent actually reasons about — it reads what the sender is asking and decides how to respond, using judgment, the same as if someone had typed the request straight into a session with it.

x — fixed recipe

A pre-signed recipe runs

The background daemon works differently: a verified, permitted email doesn't get to freely instruct anything. It can only pick which of a small set of recipes runs — recipe files that were written and digitally signed in advance. The email supplies no new instructions, only a selection.

Who's allowed to sign a recipe is a separate question from who holds x. Each running daemon has exactly one configured authorizer — a specific GPG key that every recipe file must be signed with before the daemon will load it at all. Holding x on a contact only lets that sender's mail select among the recipes the authorizer already signed; it grants no power to write new ones. And the reverse holds too — being the authorizer doesn't grant any rwx permission over anyone's mail; it only decides which recipe files are real. These are two independent locks, not a hierarchy.
Why the recipe needs that extra lock at all. Reading a message and using judgment has a safety net built in — the agent can notice something's off. Running a fixed recipe has no such net: it just executes, exactly as written. So a recipe file needs a signature check that has nothing to do with any individual email being trustworthy — it's checked once, at load time, against the one key configured as this daemon's authorizer. Skip that setup entirely and this path does nothing at all, rather than guessing at what's safe. A daemon that's configured with an authorizer key but can't actually resolve it refuses to load any recipe, never "run it anyway."

Quick reference

What's happeningCheck 1 — verified?Check 2 — granted?What happens
A session reads the mailboxShown, not required—Everything is shown, labeled by trust rung; a human or agent decides
Getting a reply sentSealed or Signed & checkedwThe agent reads the message and replies using judgment
Unattended inbox processingSealed or Signed & checkedr/wSame as above, just running on a timer instead of on request
Email triggers a background taskSealed or Signed & checkedxOne recipe signed by this daemon's authorizer runs — nothing else can
For the technically curious

Check 1 = the four-level classifier (trusted/verified/untrusted/unverified), backed by PGP signature verification and Proton's end-to-end headers. Check 2 = the per-contact rwx bits (contacts.CheckPermission) — a plain lookup with no special-cased identity, so any number of contacts can independently hold any combination. The authorizer concept is currently named owner_handle/owner_gpg_key_id in daemon.json and ownerKeyID through internal/daemon's code — that naming is being corrected to "authorizer" (tracked as beadle-4ul) because "owner" wrongly implied a general position of authority that doesn't exist anywhere else in the system. The mechanism itself, VerifySignature gating beadle-daemon's command loader (DES-034/035), is unaffected by the rename — only the name is wrong today, not the design.

Beadle — GPG-signed recipes, permission grants per sender, zero agent authority by default.

The shipping component is `beadle-email` — an MCP server for email communication via Proton Bridge with a four-level PGP trust model.

## What Beadle Is

Beadle gives an **AI agent** its own email address and mailbox — it is not a tool for managing a human's personal inbox. Once an agent has a mailbox, email becomes a channel other parties can use to instruct it, with no live session required. Everything in the trust model exists to answer one question for that channel: who is allowed to direct this agent, and how much authority does a given message actually carry.

Two independent mechanisms decide that. **There is no privileged "owner" role sitting above them** — do not model one when reasoning about this system:

1. **Message verification** — the four-level trust classification (`trusted`/`verified`/`untrusted`/`unverified`, see Trust Model below), proving how hard a given message would be to forge.
2. **Per-contact permission grants (`rwx`)** — set independently per sender, per identity (`internal/contacts.CheckPermission`). Any number of different people or systems can each hold their own combination of read/reply/execute; nobody is special by default, and a perfectly verified message from an ungranted sender still unlocks nothing.

The one place "owner" shows up in code today (`daemon.json`'s `owner_handle`/`owner_gpg_key_id`, `internal/daemon.VerifySignature`'s `ownerKeyID`) is much narrower than the word implies: it names the single GPG key that must have signed a `beadle-daemon` recipe (command) file before the daemon will load it at all — an **authorizer** for recipe files, not a general position of authority, and unrelated to anyone's `rwx` grants. That naming is wrong and is being corrected (tracked as `beadle-4ul`); until it lands, read every "owner" in `internal/daemon` as "recipe authorizer," nothing more.
